section.title: Sodom Destroyed
section.sectionRationale: The judgment Abraham had pleaded against now falls. The chapter exposes the depth of Sodom's wickedness, the reluctant rescue of Lot by grace alone, and the sobering aftermath in the cave. It stands throughout Scripture as a fixed warning of judgment and a display of mercy that saves the undeserving.
section.thesis: God's patience with wickedness has a limit, and when it comes His judgment is real and total; yet He rescues Lot not for Lot's worthiness but because He remembered Abraham, showing that salvation from wrath is always by grace.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Lot's dangerous hospitality and the assault on his house; the urgent flight from the doomed city; the fire from heaven and Lot's wife; and the grim aftermath in the cave.

verses.text: Now the two {{malak|angels}} arrived at Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gateway of the city. When Lot saw them, he got up to meet them, bowed facedown,

and said, “My lords, please turn aside into the house of your servant; wash your feet and spend the night. Then you can rise early and go on your way.” “No,” they answered, “we will spend the night in the square.”
But Lot insisted so strongly that they followed him into his house. He prepared a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
Before they had gone to bed, all the men of the city of Sodom, both young and old, surrounded the house.
They called out to Lot, saying, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Send them out to us so we can have relations with them!”
Lot went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him.
“Please, my brothers,” he pleaded, “don’t do such a wicked thing!

Look, I have two daughters who have never slept with a man. Let me bring them to you, and you can do to them as you please. But do not do anything to these men, for they have come under the protection of my roof.”

“Get out of the way!” they replied. And they declared, “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge! Now we will treat you worse than them.” And they pressed in on Lot and moved in to break down the door.
But the men inside reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door.
And they struck the men at the entrance, young and old, with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.

units.label: Flee, and do not look back

verses.text: Then the two men said to Lot, “Do you have anyone else here, a son-in-law, your sons or daughters, or anyone else in the city who belongs to you? Get them out of here,
because we are about to destroy this place. For the {{outcry|outcry}} to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent us to destroy it.”

So Lot went out and spoke to the sons-in-law who were pledged in marriage to his daughters. “Get up,” he said. “Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city!” But his sons-in-law thought he was joking.
At daybreak the angels hurried Lot along, saying, “Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be swept away in the punishment of the city.”
But when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters. And they led them safely out of the city, because of the LORD’s {{chemlah|compassion}} for them.
As soon as the men had brought them out, one of them said, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain! Flee to the mountains, or you will be swept away!”
But Lot replied, “No, my lords, please!
Your servant has indeed found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness by sparing my life. But I cannot run to the mountains; the disaster will overtake me, and I will die.
Look, there is a town nearby where I can flee, and it is a small place. Please let me flee there, is it not a small place? Then my life will be saved.”
“Very well,” he answered, “I will grant this request as well, and will not demolish the town you indicate.
Hurry! Run there quickly, for I cannot do anything until you reach it.” That is why the town was called Zoar.
And by the time the sun had risen over the land, Lot had reached Zoar.
Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, from the LORD out of the heavens.
Thus He destroyed these cities and the entire plain, including all the inhabitants of the cities and everything that grew on the ground.
But Lot’s wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
Early the next morning, Abraham got up and returned to the place where he had stood before the LORD.
He looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the plain, and he saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.
So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, He {{zakar|remembered}} Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.
Lot and his two daughters left Zoar and settled in the mountains, for he was afraid to stay in Zoar, where they lived in a cave.
One day the older daughter said to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to sleep with us, as is the custom over all the earth.
Come, let us get our father drunk with wine so we can sleep with him and preserve his line.”
So that night they got their father drunk with wine, and the firstborn went in and slept with her father; he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up.

The next day the older daughter said to the younger, “Look, I slept with my father last night. Let us get him drunk with wine again tonight so you can go in and sleep with him and we can preserve our father’s line.”
So again that night they got their father drunk with wine, and the younger daughter went in and slept with him; he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up.
Thus both of Lot’s daughters became pregnant by their father.
The older daughter gave birth to a son and named him Moab. He is the father of the Moabites of today.
The younger daughter also gave birth to a son, and she named him Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites of today.

malak.gloss: A messenger or angel. The two who were with the LORD at Mamre now come to Sodom as agents of both rescue and judgment. They deliver Lot and then destroy the city, showing that the same visitation brings salvation to some and ruin to others.

outcry.gloss: A cry, an outcry, often the scream of the oppressed for help. Sodom's sin has produced such a cry to the LORD that judgment is sent. The word links Sodom's violence to the suffering it caused and shows that God hears and answers the cries of the wronged.

chemlah.gloss: Compassion, pity, sparing mercy. Lot is saved not because he is bold or ready, but because of the LORD's compassion; the angels seize his hand while he lingers. It names the tender pity of God that rescues the hesitant and undeserving.

zakar.gloss: To remember, to call to mind and act upon. God remembered Abraham, and so Lot was brought out. To remember in Scripture is not mere recollection but faithful action; Lot's rescue is credited to God honoring His covenant friend's intercession.

basic.context: The two angels who left Abraham arrive in Sodom, and the city's wickedness is laid bare in the mob at Lot's door. The judgment Abraham pleaded against now falls. The key question is why Lot is saved at all, and the answer is grace: God remembered Abraham.
basic.hermeneutics: This is sober history, and Scripture treats it as a fixed example of judgment and of rescue. The narrative describes terrible things, including Lot's offer of his daughters and the later incest, without approving them. The debate is over Lot's spiritual state, but the clear point is that salvation from wrath is by mercy, not merit.
basic.originalLanguages: The two are called angels, messengers who both rescue and destroy. Sodom's sin has raised an outcry, the cry of the oppressed, to the LORD. Lot is led out because of God's compassion, His sparing pity, and above all because God remembered Abraham, a remembering that always leads to action.
basic.typology: The fire that falls on Sodom becomes a standing picture of final judgment. Lot dragged out by the hand pictures salvation that grips the reluctant. Lot's wife looking back warns of a heart still bound to the world under judgment.
basic.christ: Jesus points to this day to warn of His coming: remember Lot's wife, and as it was in the days of Lot, so it will be. He is the greater rescuer who bears the fire of judgment Himself so His people can be brought out safely.
basic.god: God is holy and just, and His patience with evil is not endless. Yet He is compassionate, seizing the hand of a hesitating man, and faithful, remembering His covenant with Abraham even when saving Abraham's undeserving nephew.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Peter 2 and Jude cite Sodom as an example of judgment and Lot as rescued. Luke 17 has Jesus recall these days and Lot's wife. Deuteronomy remembers the overthrow of the cities.
basic.oneStory: Sodom shows that judgment is real and that rescue from it is by grace alone. Lot is saved because God remembered Abraham, a foretaste of how all who are saved are spared for the sake of Another. The story presses on toward Christ, who takes the fire so His people can flee to safety.

context.literary:
Genesis 19 is written to be read against Genesis 18, and nearly every detail of the opening echoes the meal at Mamre. Abraham sat at his tent entrance "in the heat of the day," Genesis 18:1; Lot sits "in the gateway of the city" in the evening, verse 1. Abraham ran to meet his guests and bowed; Lot gets up and bows facedown. Both offer water to wash the visitors' feet, Genesis 18:4 and 19:2. Both provide a meal, and both use the language of servanthood. Then the parallels break. At Mamre the visitors bring the promise of a son; in Sodom the whole male population comes to the door to abuse them. Sarah laughed at the promise; Lot's sons-in-law think his warning is a joke, verse 14.

The chapter moves in four stages. Verses 1 to 11 take place at night in and around Lot's house, climaxing in the mob's attempt to break the door and the angels' act of blinding. Verses 12 to 23 run from night to dawn, full of imperatives: get them out, get up, take your wife, run for your lives, do not look back, hurry. Lot's hesitation, verse 16, and his bargaining over Zoar, verses 18 to 20, stand in contrast to the urgency. Verses 24 to 29 are the judgment itself, told in only a few sentences, with a double viewpoint: Lot's wife looks back from the plain, and Abraham looks down from the hills. Verses 30 to 38 move to a cave in the mountains, where the story ends not with triumph but with drunkenness, incest and the births of Moab and Ammon.

The chapter also mirrors the flood. A whole society is destroyed for its violence and corruption; a righteous man and his family are brought out; God "remembered" the one who is spared, Genesis 8:1 and 19:29; and the rescued patriarch then becomes drunk on wine, and his children act shamefully, Genesis 9:20-23. Jesus pairs the two events explicitly, "as it was in the days of Noah" and "the same in the days of Lot," Luke 17:26-29, and 2 Peter 2:5-7 does the same.

Verse 29 is the theological centre. After the fire, the narrator does not dwell on Sodom's ruin but explains Lot's escape: God "remembered Abraham." The rescue is not credited to Lot at all.
context.historical:
Lot "was sitting in the gateway of the city," verse 1. In the ancient Near East the city gate was the place of business and judgment, where elders sat to hear cases, Ruth 4:1 and Deuteronomy 21:19. Lot's seat there suggests that he had risen to some standing in Sodom, which makes the mob's sneer in verse 9, "This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge!" especially pointed. He belonged enough to sit at the gate but was still an outsider when it mattered.

Travellers without hosts would often spend the night in the open square, which is what the angels propose, verse 2. Lot's insistence shows he knew the danger. Judges 19 describes almost the same scene in the Israelite town of Gibeah: a traveller in the square, an old man who takes him in, a mob that surrounds the house demanding to "have relations with him," and a host who offers women instead, Judges 19:15 and 19:22-25. The deliberate echo shows that Israel itself could become Sodom.

The location of the cities is uncertain. The biblical text places them in "the plain of the Jordan," once "well watered like the garden of the LORD," Genesis 13:10, near the Valley of Siddim with its "tar pits," Genesis 14:10. Traditional identification has placed them near the southern end of the Dead Sea, where a salt ridge is still known in modern times as Mount Sodom, while some have proposed sites north-east of the sea. What is clear is that the region became a byword for desolation, a land of "sulfur and salt, unsown and unproductive," Deuteronomy 29:23.

Moab and Ammon, the peoples born in the cave, were Israel's neighbours east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. God gave them their lands as "descendants of Lot" and forbade Israel to harass them, Deuteronomy 2:9 and 2:19. Yet they often opposed Israel: Eglon of Moab oppressed Israel, Judges 3:12-14, and Nahash the Ammonite threatened Jabesh-gilead, 1 Samuel 11:1-2. Deuteronomy 23:3 excluded them from the assembly. For the first hearers, the chapter explained the origins of peoples they knew well, and did so with a story of shame.
context.canonical:
Sodom's destruction becomes the Bible's standard measure of total judgment. Moses warns that a rebellious Israel will become like "the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah," Deuteronomy 29:23, and calls Israel's corruption "the vine of Sodom," Deuteronomy 32:32. Isaiah addresses Jerusalem's leaders as "rulers of Sodom," Isaiah 1:10, and says that without a remnant "we would have become like Sodom," Isaiah 1:9. Jeremiah says Jerusalem's prophets are "all like Sodom to Me," Jeremiah 23:14, and Lamentations says Jerusalem's punishment is greater than Sodom's, Lamentations 4:6. Babylon, Edom, Moab and Ammon are all threatened with an overthrow "like Sodom and Gomorrah," Isaiah 13:19, Jeremiah 49:18 and Zephaniah 2:9. Amos says God overthrew some of Israel "as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah," and they were "like a firebrand snatched from a blaze," Amos 4:11, the very image of Lot's rescue.

Ezekiel adds a surprising note. He names Sodom's sins as arrogance, excess and neglect of the poor as well as "abominations," Ezekiel 16:49-50, and then says God will one day "restore Sodom and her daughters," Ezekiel 16:53.

In the New Testament Jesus says that towns rejecting His messengers will fare worse than Sodom on the day of judgment, Matthew 10:14-15 and 11:23-24. He uses the days of Lot as a picture of the suddenness of His coming and warns, "Remember Lot's wife!" Luke 17:28-32. Peter cites Sodom as "an example of what is coming on the ungodly," and Lot as proof that "the Lord knows how to rescue the godly," 2 Peter 2:6-9. Jude 7 points to the cities as a display of "the punishment of eternal fire." Revelation calls the city where the Lord was crucified "figuratively called Sodom and Egypt," Revelation 11:8, and uses the imagery of fire, sulfur and rising smoke for final judgment, Revelation 14:10-11 and 19:3.

The descendants of the cave also have a canonical afterlife. Ruth the Moabite becomes the great-grandmother of David, Ruth 4:13-17, and is named in the genealogy of Jesus, Matthew 1:5. Naamah the Ammonite was the mother of King Rehoboam, 1 Kings 14:21.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that the Judge of all the earth does what is right. Chapter 18 established that God would spare Sodom for ten righteous people; chapter 19 shows that the city's wickedness was total. The whole male population, "both young and old," verse 4, surrounds the house. The investigation God promised in Genesis 18:21 is carried out, and the verdict is beyond dispute.

He also wanted Israel to understand that rescue from judgment is by grace. Lot is not presented as a hero. He hesitates, bargains, and fails to persuade even his own family. The angels must seize his hand, verse 16, and the narrator explains that it was "because of the LORD's compassion for them." Verse 29 then gives the deeper reason: God "remembered Abraham." Israel was meant to learn that their own survival, too, rested on God's covenant memory, not on their merit, Exodus 2:24.

Third, Moses wanted Israel to feel the danger of living too close to Sodom. Lot chose the plain for its appearance, Genesis 13:10-12, moved into the city, and took a seat in its gate. The cost was his wife, his sons-in-law, his possessions and finally his dignity in the cave.

Finally, the closing verses explain the origins of Moab and Ammon. They are relatives, descendants of Abraham's nephew, which is why Israel was not to take their land. But they were born of a shameful act that echoed the corruption of the city Lot had left.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this chapter records sin without approving it. Lot's offer of his daughters to the mob, verse 8, is not held up as an example of hospitality but as a sign of how deeply Sodom had bent his judgment. The incest of verses 30 to 38 is narrated flatly, without comment, but the context of Leviticus 18 and the names of the sons make the narrator's view plain. None of these acts is prescriptive.

The chapter's lasting instructions are drawn out by the New Testament. Jesus uses it to call for readiness and detachment, "Remember Lot's wife," Luke 17:32, and "Whoever tries to save his life will lose it," Luke 17:33. Peter uses it to assure believers that God knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgment, 2 Peter 2:9. Jude uses it as a warning against those who "turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality," Jude 1:4-7.

The chapter also carries a warning for believers who live among the ungodly: like Lot, they can be "tormented" by lawlessness, 2 Peter 2:8, and yet slowly absorbed by it. The call is to flee what God is judging and not to look back.

debates.question: Was Lot a righteous man or a compromised one?

views.label: Righteous yet deeply compromised
views.case: Peter calls Lot "a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless," 2 Peter 2:7-8, and the text shows him welcoming the strangers, protecting them at personal risk and warning his family. At the same time his choices, his lingering, verse 16, and his readiness to sacrifice his daughters show a faith badly eroded by the city.

views.label: A cautionary figure of worldliness
views.case: Genesis itself never calls Lot righteous. It highlights his choice of the plain for its appearance, Genesis 13:10-12, his hesitation, his bargaining over Zoar, and the ruin of his household. On this view the narrative presents Lot as a warning of what it costs to pitch one's tent toward Sodom, and Peter's word "righteous" refers to his standing before God and his distress at sin rather than to the quality of his life.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree Lot is saved by grace, not by his own goodness, and the text makes that point explicitly in verses 16 and 29. His story warns against worldliness even as it displays God's mercy toward the undeserving.

debates.question: What was the sin of Sodom?

views.label: Sexual violence and immorality
views.case: The chapter's central scene is the attempted gang rape of the visitors, verse 5, where "have relations" translates the verb to know used of sexual intimacy in verse 8. Jude 7 says the cities "indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh," and 2 Peter 2:7 speaks of their "depraved conduct." Many read the sin as sexual in nature, including same-sex acts and violence.

views.label: Pride, oppression and inhospitality
views.case: Ezekiel 16:49 names Sodom's iniquity as arrogance, excess and complacency, and says "they did not help the poor and needy." The "outcry" of Genesis 18:20-21 is the cry of the oppressed. Jesus links Sodom to towns that refuse to welcome His messengers, Matthew 10:14-15. On this view the core sin is social injustice and hostility to the stranger.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Many interpreters read the biblical witness as a composite. Ezekiel continues, "they were haughty and committed abominations before Me," Ezekiel 16:50, placing pride and abominable acts side by side. The assault on the guests is the supreme expression of a city that despised the vulnerable and abandoned God's order for sexuality.

debates.bearing: Scripture does not reduce Sodom to a single sin. The mob scene shows violence, sexual depravity and hatred of the stranger converging in one act, and the prophets and apostles each draw out a different strand. The text warns against any reading that uses Sodom to condemn others while ignoring the pride and neglect of the poor Ezekiel names.

debates.question: Why does verse 24 say the LORD rained down fire "from the LORD out of the heavens"?

views.label: Emphatic Hebrew style
views.case: Hebrew narrative sometimes repeats a noun where English would use a pronoun. On this reading the verse simply stresses that the fire came directly from the LORD, not from any natural force or other god.

views.label: A hint of distinction within God
views.case: Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr read the verse as the LORD on earth, who had spoken with Abraham, bringing judgment from the LORD in heaven, and saw in it a glimpse of the Son and the Father. They linked it with other texts where the LORD is distinguished from the LORD.

debates.bearing: The grammar does not require the second reading, and the verse's main point is that the judgment was God's own act. Yet in a chapter where the LORD has been present on earth, Genesis 18:22, the phrasing leaves room for the fuller revelation of the triune God that the New Testament makes explicit.

study.originalLanguages:
The mob's demand in verse 5, "so we can have relations with them," uses yada, to know, the verb Genesis uses for sexual intimacy from Genesis 4:1 onward. Lot's reply in verse 8 uses the same verb: his daughters "have never slept with a man," literally have not known a man. The same verb was used in the previous chapter for God's choosing of Abraham, "I have known him," Genesis 18:19, and for God's investigation, "I will find out," Genesis 18:21. God knows in love and in justice; Sodom wants to know in violence.

In verse 3 Lot "insisted so strongly" that the visitors came in, and in verse 9 the men "pressed in" on Lot. Both use the verb patsar, to press or urge. Lot presses his guests to safety; the mob presses toward the door to harm them. The same word frames the danger.

The mob's insult in verse 9 uses a doubled construction of shaphat, to judge: wayyishpot shaphot, "he keeps on playing the judge." The root is the one Abraham used for God as "the Judge of all the earth," Genesis 18:25. The men of Sodom sneer at a foreigner for judging them, while the true Judge's messengers stand inside the house.

When Lot warns his sons-in-law, they think he is "joking," metsacheq, verse 14. The word comes from tsachaq, to laugh, the root of Isaac's name. In chapter 18 laughter met the promise of life; here it meets the warning of death.

Lot "hesitated," verse 16, wayyitmahmah, a form that suggests lingering or dawdling. The psalmist uses the same verb when he says, "I hurried without hesitating to keep Your commandments," Psalm 119:60. The angels' response is to seize the hands of all four, "because of the LORD's compassion," chemlat YHWH, His sparing pity.

The verb malat, to escape or slip away, runs through verses 17 to 22: "Run for your lives," "let me flee there," "Run there quickly." Lot's request is that the town be spared because it is mits'ar, "a small place," verse 20, and the BSB footnote explains that Zoar means small. The name of the town is a memorial of his plea. Zoar was earlier called Bela, Genesis 14:2.

The verb for the destruction is haphak, to overturn, verses 21, 25 and 29, where the noun hahaphekah is rendered "the catastrophe." It describes a complete reversal, the land turned upside down. It becomes the fixed term for Sodom's fate in later Scripture: the LORD "overthrew" the cities, Deuteronomy 29:23, and "as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah," Amos 4:11, Jeremiah 49:18 and 50:40.

The fire is "rained down," verse 24, from the verb matar. The same verb is used for the hail that fell on Egypt, Exodus 9:23, and, in a striking contrast, for the manna: "I will rain down bread from heaven for you," Exodus 16:4. God can rain judgment or provision from the same heaven.

Lot's wife "looked back," verse 26, wattabbet, the same verb the angel used in verse 17, "Do not look back." The Hebrew says she looked "from behind him," me'acharav, which suggests she was trailing behind Lot, lingering at the edge of the city. By contrast, Abraham "looked down," verse 28, wayyashqeph, the same verb used when the visitors "looked out over Sodom" in Genesis 18:16.

Finally, the BSB footnotes explain that Moab sounds like "from my father" and Ben-ammi means "son of my people." The names themselves preserve the memory of their origin.

typology.type: Fire and sulfur falling on Sodom, Genesis 19:24-25
typology.fulfillment: The overthrow of Sodom is sudden, complete and from heaven. Jesus makes it the pattern of the day He is revealed: "fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all. It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed," Luke 17:29-30. Jude 7 calls it a display of "the punishment of eternal fire," and Revelation uses its language for final judgment, Revelation 14:10-11 and 20:10. The escalation is from a regional judgment to a universal one. Christ delivers His people from that coming wrath, 1 Thessalonians 1:10, by bearing judgment Himself.

typology.type: Lot seized by the hand and brought out, Genesis 19:16
typology.fulfillment: Lot hesitates, and the angels grasp his hand and lead him out because of the LORD's compassion. This is a vivid picture of grace that does not wait for the reluctant to find their own way. Christ "gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age," Galatians 1:4, and God "has rescued us from the dominion of darkness," Colossians 1:13. Jude 23 speaks of "snatching them from the fire," and Amos 4:11 of a "firebrand snatched from a blaze." The type falls short because the angels brought Lot out of a city; Christ brings His people out of death itself.

typology.type: Lot's wife looking back and becoming a pillar of salt, Genesis 19:26
typology.fulfillment: She was brought out but did not leave in her heart. Jesus commands, "Remember Lot's wife!" Luke 17:32, in the context of warning against turning back for possessions when He comes. He also says, "No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God," Luke 9:62. The type is a negative one: she shows that nearness to rescue is not the same as salvation, and that a heart still bound to what God is judging can be lost at the very edge of safety.

typology.type: Lot saved because God remembered Abraham, Genesis 19:29
typology.fulfillment: Lot is rescued not for his own righteousness but for the sake of another, the man who stood before the LORD and pleaded. This points to the deepest pattern of the gospel: believers are saved for the sake of Christ, who intercedes for them, Romans 8:34, and because God remembers His covenant, Luke 1:72-73. The escalation is that Abraham could only plead; Christ both pleads and pays. Lot was spared from a judgment on one city; believers are spared from the final judgment "through Him," Romans 5:9.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the words of Jesus Himself. He takes the day of Sodom as a picture of His coming: "It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all. It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed," Luke 17:28-30. What strikes Jesus is not only the wickedness of Sodom but its ordinariness. Life went on as normal until the last day. His warning, "Remember Lot's wife!" Luke 17:32, is addressed to disciples, not to Sodom. The danger He names is that of being rescued in body while the heart looks back.

It leads to Christ through the logic of rescue. Lot is not saved because he deserved it. He is dragged out by the hand because of God's compassion, verse 16, and because God remembered Abraham, verse 29. That is the shape of the gospel. Believers are rescued "from the coming wrath" by Jesus, 1 Thessalonians 1:10, not because of their worth but because of His. Just as Lot was spared for the sake of the one who interceded, believers are spared for the sake of Christ, who "is interceding for us," Romans 8:34, and whose blood has justified us, Romans 5:9.

It leads to Christ through the delay of judgment. The angel tells Lot, "I cannot do anything until you reach it," verse 22. Judgment waits until the righteous are safe. Peter draws the same lesson about the final day: the Lord "is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish," 2 Peter 3:9, and He "knows how to rescue the godly from trials," 2 Peter 2:9. Christ is the one in whom that safety is found.

It leads to Christ through the fire itself. The fire of Sodom is a picture of the wrath that rests on sin, John 3:36. At the cross the Son took that wrath on Himself. He was the righteous one numbered with the transgressors, so that those who flee to Him are not consumed. Hebrews speaks of believers "who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us," Hebrews 6:18, the language of Lot running for his life, now applied to faith in Christ.

It leads to Christ even through the cave. From the incest of Lot's daughters comes Moab, and from Moab comes Ruth, who is named in Christ's genealogy, Matthew 1:5. The line of the Messiah passes through a people born in shame. That is not a coded message hidden in Genesis, but it is a real thread the New Testament itself traces, and it shows how far the grace of God reaches.

The caution remains. Not every detail of the chapter is a picture of Christ. The angels are not Christ, and Lot is not a model saint. The link is through what the New Testament itself draws out: the certainty of judgment, the rescue of the undeserving for the sake of another, and the call to flee without looking back.
study.god:
This chapter shows the holiness of God in its most fearful form. The patience that listened to Abraham six times in chapter 18 has a limit, and when it is reached the judgment is complete: "He destroyed these cities and the entire plain, including all the inhabitants of the cities and everything that grew on the ground," verse 25. The same God who gave the plain its fertility, "well watered like the garden of the LORD," Genesis 13:10, turns it into a waste of sulfur and salt. Scripture does not soften this. "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God," Hebrews 10:31, and "our God is a consuming fire," Hebrews 12:29.

Yet the chapter shows that God's judgment is never careless. He investigated first, as He promised, Genesis 18:21. The evidence was overwhelming: the whole city came to the door. And His judgment waited for the rescue of the one family He had determined to spare: "I cannot do anything until you reach it," verse 22. The Judge of all the earth did what was right, sparing the righteous from the fate of the wicked, exactly as Abraham had asked.

God is compassionate beyond His people's deserving. Lot hesitates, and God's messengers seize him by the hand. Lot bargains for Zoar, and God grants it: "I will grant this request as well," verse 21. The word used for His compassion, chemlah, is the tender sparing pity that Isaiah 63:9 attributes to the God who "redeemed them" and "carried them all the days of old." He is patient with a weak man even in the very hour of judgment.

God is faithful to His covenant. The reason given for Lot's rescue is not Lot's goodness but that "He remembered Abraham," verse 29. This remembering is not recall of a forgotten fact but the covenant faithfulness that moves God to act, as when He remembered Noah, Genesis 8:1, Rachel, Genesis 30:22, and His covenant in Egypt, Exodus 2:24. God's promises to one person spill over as mercy to those connected with him.

God is sovereign over the heavens. The LORD "rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, from the LORD out of the heavens," verse 24. The heaven that rains judgment on Sodom is the heaven that later rains manna on Israel, Exodus 16:4. God is not bound by nature; He wields it for justice and for provision.

God's dealings with Moab and Ammon show that even in shame He does not abandon His purposes. He gives the descendants of Lot a land, Deuteronomy 2:9 and 2:19, and He brings Ruth the Moabite into the line of David and of Christ.

For worship, the chapter calls for both fear and trust. It teaches believers to take God's judgment seriously, to flee from what He condemns, and to rest in the covenant faithfulness by which He rescues the undeserving.

crossReferences.note: Lot chose the plain because it looked like the garden of the LORD, and pitched his tent toward Sodom, though its men were wicked. Genesis 19 shows where that choice led: from a tent near Sodom to a seat in its gate, and then to a cave in the mountains.

The LORD's investigation and Abraham's intercession set up this chapter. God promised to spare the city for ten righteous; the mob at Lot's door shows that not even ten could be found, and the judgment falls only after the righteous are removed.

In the Israelite town of Gibeah the wicked men surround a house and demand a guest, using almost the same words as Genesis 19:5, and a host offers women instead. The echo shows that Israel had become Sodom, and it led to near destruction of the tribe of Benjamin.

Moses warns that Israel's land could become a burning waste of sulfur and salt 'just like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew.' The judgment of Genesis 19 becomes the benchmark of covenant curse.

Ezekiel names Sodom's iniquity as arrogance, excess and complacency, failing to help the poor and needy, and committing abominations. The prophet widens the reader's view of the sins that produced the outcry of Genesis 18:20-21 and applies it to Jerusalem.

God says He overthrew some of Israel as He overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and they were like a firebrand snatched from a blaze, yet they did not return. The image recalls Lot pulled from the fire, and warns that rescue without repentance is not enough.

Jesus compares the day of His revealing to the day Lot left Sodom, when ordinary life was cut off by fire from heaven. 'Remember Lot's wife!' warns disciples not to turn back for possessions, and 'whoever tries to save his life will lose it' explains why she was lost.

Peter sets Sodom's destruction as an example of what is coming on the ungodly, and Lot's rescue as proof that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly. He calls Lot righteous and tormented by the lawlessness around him, a gracious verdict on a flawed man.

Jude says Sodom, Gomorrah and the surrounding cities indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, and are on display as an example of those who undergo the punishment of eternal fire. He uses Genesis 19 to warn those who turn grace into licence.

Jesus says that if His miracles had been done in Sodom it would have remained, and that it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for Capernaum. Rejecting Christ is worse than the sin that brought down fire on the city.

God remembered Noah and the creatures in the ark, and the waters subsided. Genesis 19:29 uses the same language, God remembered Abraham, to explain Lot's escape. In both judgments God's covenant memory is the reason anyone survives.

Ruth the Moabite, a descendant of the son born in the cave, marries Boaz and becomes the great-grandmother of David. The people born in the shame of Genesis 19:37 are brought into the royal line and, through Matthew 1:5, into the genealogy of Jesus.

study.oneStory:
Genesis has already told one story of total judgment. The flood swept away a world whose wickedness was great and whose every thought was evil, Genesis 6:5, and God preserved one righteous family. After the flood God promised never again to destroy the earth by water, Genesis 9:11, but He did not promise that judgment itself would cease. Sodom shows that it has not. The overthrow of the cities of the plain proves that the God who made the world still judges it, and that His patience, however long, is not endless.

The chapter also answers the question Abraham raised in Genesis 18: will the Judge of all the earth sweep away the righteous with the wicked? He will not. He brings Lot out first, and only then does the fire fall. And He does it because He remembered Abraham, the man through whom all nations would be blessed. The promise to Abraham is already at work, protecting even an undeserving relative from judgment.

The chapter then sets a pattern that runs through the rest of Scripture. Sodom becomes the name for every society ripe for judgment, including Israel and Jerusalem. The prophets warn that God's own people can become Sodom, and the story of Gibeah proves them right. At the same time, the rescue of Lot sets a pattern of grace: the remnant saved not by their own strength but by the covenant faithfulness of God. The people born in shame from Lot's cave are not forgotten either, and a Moabite woman becomes the ancestor of Israel's king.

The story comes to rest in Christ. He speaks of Sodom to warn of His coming, and He is the one who rescues His people from the wrath to come, 1 Thessalonians 1:10. He is the true intercessor for whose sake God remembers the undeserving, and He is the one who bore the fire of judgment at the cross so that His people could flee to Him and live.

The new creation is the final answer to Sodom. There will be no outcry in the new Jerusalem, because there will be "no more death or mourning or crying or pain," Revelation 21:4. There will be no more mob at the door, because "nothing unclean will ever enter it," Revelation 21:27. And where the smoke of Sodom rose like the smoke of a furnace, Genesis 19:28, the city of God will shine with His glory, and "by its light the nations will walk," Revelation 21:24.

quiz.q: Why was Lot rescued from the destruction of Sodom?

options.text: Because of God's compassion and because He remembered Abraham.
options.note: The rescue rests on grace and God's covenant with Abraham, not Lot's merit.

options.text: Because Lot was bold and ready to flee at once.
options.note: In fact Lot hesitated and had to be dragged out; the rescue was by mercy.

options.text: Because Lot had converted the city to righteousness.
options.note: The city was wholly given to wickedness; Lot saved none of it.

options.text: Because Lot bargained his way out with the angels.
options.note: He bargained about where to flee, but his deliverance came from God's compassion.

quiz.q: What happened to Lot's wife, and why does it matter?

options.text: She looked back and became a pillar of salt, a warning against clinging to the doomed world.
options.note: Jesus says, remember Lot's wife, Luke 17:32.

options.text: She was left behind in the city by accident.
options.note: She was brought out but looked back; it was not mere accident.

options.text: She refused to leave and stayed in Sodom.
options.note: She did leave, but turned back with her heart still in the city.

options.text: She led the family safely to the mountains.
options.note: She perished on the way; she did not lead them to safety.

quiz.q: How did the men of Sodom respond to Lot's visitors?

options.text: They surrounded the house and demanded to abuse the men.
options.note: Their assault exposes the wickedness that provoked judgment.

options.text: They welcomed the strangers with their own hospitality.
options.note: Only Lot showed hospitality; the city showed violent hostility.

options.text: They ignored the visitors entirely.
options.note: Far from ignoring them, they violently sought them out.

options.text: They repented when they heard of the coming judgment.
options.note: They hardened themselves and pressed in even after being struck blind.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use the destruction of Sodom?

options.text: As an example of judgment on the ungodly and of God rescuing the godly.
options.note: 2 Peter 2 and Jude cite both the judgment and Lot's rescue.

options.text: As proof that God never sends judgment.
options.note: The opposite; it is the standard example that judgment is real.

options.text: As a myth with no bearing on later teaching.
options.note: Jesus, Peter, and Jude all treat it as real and instructive.

options.text: As evidence that the wicked are always spared.
options.note: The wicked were destroyed; only Lot's family was spared, by grace.

quiz.q: What does it mean that God remembered Abraham?

options.text: God acted on His covenant faithfulness, bringing Lot out for Abraham's sake.
options.note: Biblical remembering is faithful, saving action.

options.text: God suddenly recalled a promise He had forgotten.
options.note: God does not forget; remembering here means He acted on His covenant.

options.text: God rewarded Lot for his own righteousness.
options.note: The rescue is tied to Abraham, not to Lot's merit.

options.text: God changed His mind about judging Sodom.
options.note: Sodom was still destroyed; only Lot was brought out.

questions: The angels had to seize Lot's hand because he lingered. Where are you hesitating over something God is clearly calling you to leave behind?
Lot was saved because God remembered Abraham, not because Lot deserved it. How does it humble and comfort you to know that salvation is by grace, not merit?
Jesus said, 'Remember Lot's wife.' Is there something in the world under judgment that your heart keeps looking back to?
Sodom's sin raised an outcry that God heard and answered. How does it change your view of injustice to know that God hears the cries of the oppressed?
Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom and it cost his family dearly. What small compromises might be pulling your household in a direction you would not choose?

translationNotes.note: From the LORD out of the heavens stresses that the judgment came directly from God.
Zoar means small; the name preserves Lot's plea that the town was only a small place.
Moab sounds like the Hebrew for from my father, and Ben-ammi means son of my people; the names quietly mark the origin of these nations in the cave.
